table.text: Students were eligible to participate if they were enrolled in the introduction to psychology research pools at the two schools.
Given the overlap between those two categories, a total of n = 77 participants were excluded, leaving a sample of N = 333 who completed sufficient measures to be included in the analysis.
Study 2 was conducted through Prolific in November of 2025, with Qualtrics as the survey platform.
Potential participants were required to be enrolled as undergraduate students in a twoor four-year program and had to be based in the United States.
Participants were compensated $3.75 USD through Prolific upon completion of the nine-minute survey.

Of those, n = 188 completed the survey in under 240 seconds (an impossible speed), n = 95 did not provide their age or other critical demographic information, n = 88 failed one or more of the Prolific and Qualtrics bot/AI completer checks, and n = 455 indicated that they were not currently undergraduate students.
Given the overlap between those categories, a total of 601 participants were excluded, leaving a sample of N = 1,555 who completed sufficient measures to be included in the analysis.

To reduce participant burden, we used a planned missingness design (Graham et al., 2006). (Graham et al., 2006) All participants completed a core battery: demographic questions, the depression and anxiety subscales from the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale (Henry & Crawford, 2005), the Sleep Condition Indicator (SCI) (Espie et al., 2014), and the first four items of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) (Buysse et al., 1989).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: Insomnia is strongly associated with symptoms of depression and anxiety during emerging adulthood, yet the mechanisms underlying these relationships remain poorly understood.
Numerous constructs have been proposed as potential explanatory pathways, but few have been systematically screened and independently replicated.

This study applied a structured associational variable screening approach to identify and replicate candidate constructs associated with relationships connecting insomnia and depression and anxiety in emerging adults.
Methods: Data were drawn from two independent samples of emerging adults.
Study 1 (N = 333) provided exploratory analyses and Study 2 (N = 1,555) provided independent confirmation.
Insomnia symptoms were assessed using the Sleep Condition Indicator (SCI) and depression and anxiety symptoms using the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS).
Candidate associative variables included psychological inflexibility, emotion regulation difficulties, behavioral and experiential avoidance, maladaptive sleep-related behaviors and attitudes.

Following Weems et al. (2025), candidates were evaluated using sequential analyses of zero-order associations, multivariable associations and incremental explanatory power (ΔR²), attenuation of the sleepsymptom association, equivalence under reversal of the proposed associative pathway, and moderation.

In Study 1, emotion regulation difficulties, psychological inflexibility, and behavioral avoidance met screening criteria as potential path variables between insomnia and depression, while emotion regulation difficulties and psychological inflexibility met criteria as potential path variables between insomnia and anxiety.
These candidate associations were replicated in Study 2.
For depression, emotion regulation difficulties (ΔR² = .277), psychological inflexibility (ΔR² = .286), and behavioral avoidance (ΔR² = .122) demonstrated substantial incremental explanatory power.

For anxiety, emotion regulation difficulties (ΔR² = .175) and psychological inflexibility (ΔR² = .182) met all screening criteria, with internalizing demonstrating the largest incremental contribution.
Moderation models were estimated but consistently explained negligible additional variance (ΔR² ≤ .006).

Conclusions: Across exploratory and confirmatory samples, psychological inflexibility and emotion regulation difficulties emerged as consistent candidate associative variables linking insomnia with both depressive and anxiety symptoms.
Behavioral avoidance additionally emerged for depression.

Although the cross-sectional design precludes causal or mechanistic inference, these findings narrow a broad set of potential explanatory constructs and identify promising candidates for longitudinal and experimental research examining relationships between sleep disturbance and depression and anxiety during emerging adulthood.
Emerging adulthood is a period of heightened vulnerability to sleep disturbance, depression, and anxiety (Arnett, 2000; Suvisaari et al., 2009; Taber-Thomas & Perez-Edgar, 2015).

text.text: The transition from adolescence into adulthood is accompanied by substantial changes in social roles, educational and occupational demands, relationships, living environments, and independence over health behaviors, while neurobiological and circadian development continues to shape patterns of sleep and emotional functioning.

Against this backdrop, symptoms of depression and anxiety are highly prevalent among emerging adults (Lipson et al., 2022; Roy et al., 2025; The Healthy Minds Network, 2024) and represent major contributors to functional impairment, reduced quality of life, and suicide risk (Crowley et al., 2007; Dahl & Lewin, 2002; Gaultney, 2010; Hershner & Chervin, 2014; Lund et al., 2010; Taylor et al., 2013).

text.text: Sleep difficulties are similarly common during this developmental period, with young adults frequently experiencing insomnia symptoms, insufficient sleep, irregular sleep-wake schedules, and poor sleep quality.

Identifying factors that are associated with co-occurrence of sleep disturbance and internalizing symptoms and potentially to the progression from sleep disturbance to internalizing disorders during emerging adulthood is an important public health and clinical priority.

A substantial literature demonstrates robust associations among disturbed sleep and both depression and anxiety (Baglioni et al., 2011; Blaxton et al., 2017; Breslau et al., 1996; Buysse et al., 2008; Pigeon et al., 2008).

text.text: Insomnia is among the strongest prospective predictors of depression, predicting first onset, worsening symptoms, and recurrence even after accounting for baseline depressive symptoms (Baglioni et al., 2011; Cho et al., 2008; Gallo et al., 2020; Li et al., 2016).

text.text: Sleep disturbance may precede depressive episodes by months or years, and persistent sleep problems are associated with more severe and chronic courses of depression.

Sleep disturbance is also strongly associated with anxiety symptoms and disorders (Richards et al., 2020; Staner, 2003), and longitudinal evidence suggests bidirectional relationships in which poor sleep predicts subsequent anxiety while anxiety-related arousal and worry further interfere with sleep (Kalmbach et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2024).

text.text: During emerging adulthood, these relationships may be particularly consequential because shifting developmental, academic, occupational, and interpersonal demands can simultaneously disrupt sleep and increase vulnerability to internalizing symptoms.
Importantly, the relationship between poor sleep and internalizing psychopathology appears to extend beyond their concurrent symptom overlap.
Experimental and interventional research suggests that manipulating sleep can produce changes in emotional functioning.
Experimental sleep loss results in reduced positive affect, increased anxiety, and increased depressive symptoms (Palmer et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Experimental sleep loss results in reduced positive affect, increased anxiety, and increased depressive symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Palmer et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), the first-line treatment for insomnia, (Qaseem et al., 2016) reliably improves sleep and has also been associated with reductions in depressive and anxiety symptoms (Bei et al., 2018; Blom et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2017; Furukawa et al., 2024; Gebara et al., 2018; Irwin et al., 2022; Suh et al., 2013; Ubara et al., 2022).

text.text: Treatment of insomnia may reduce risk for subsequent depression, including among individuals without clinically significant depression at treatment initiation (Cheng et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Treatment of insomnia may reduce risk for subsequent depression, including among individuals without clinically significant depression at treatment initiation <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Cheng et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This literature suggests that sleep may represent a modifiable contributor to internalizing psychopathology rather than simply a correlate or consequence of psychological distress.
However, substantially less is known about the psychological processes that may account for these relationships.
Several candidate processes may plausibly contribute to associations among sleep disturbance, depression, and anxiety.
Emotion regulation difficulties represent one particularly compelling candidate.

Adequate sleep supports cognitive and affective regulatory functioning, whereas sleep disruption is associated with increased emotional reactivity, reduced regulatory capacity, and greater difficulty recovering from negative emotional experiences (Goldstein & Walker, 2014; Palmer & Alfano, 2017).
text.formatted: Adequate sleep supports cognitive and affective regulatory functioning, whereas sleep disruption is associated with increased emotional reactivity, reduced regulatory capacity, and greater difficulty recovering from negative emotional experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Goldstein & Walker, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Palmer & Alfano, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Difficulties regulating emotions, in turn, are strongly implicated in both depression and anxiety (Cisler & Olatunji, 2012; Visted et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Difficulties regulating emotions, in turn, are strongly implicated in both depression and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Cisler & Olatunji, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Visted et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, individuals experiencing poor sleep may become increasingly vulnerable to internalizing symptoms in part because they have greater difficulty modulating emotional responses to everyday stressors.
Psychological inflexibility and experiential avoidance may represent additional transdiagnostic processes connecting sleep with internalizing symptoms (Pantesco & Schanke, 2025; Zakiei et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Psychological inflexibility and experiential avoidance may represent additional transdiagnostic processes connecting sleep with internalizing symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Pantesco & Schanke, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Zakiei et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Psychological flexibility refers broadly to the capacity to remain in contact with difficult internal experiences while adapting behavior in accordance with situational demands and personally meaningful goals (Doorley et al., 2020; Kashdan, 2010).
text.formatted: Psychological flexibility refers broadly to the capacity to remain in contact with difficult internal experiences while adapting behavior in accordance with situational demands and personally meaningful goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Doorley et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Kashdan, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, psychological inflexibility and experiential avoidance involve rigid efforts to control, suppress, or escape unwanted thoughts, emotions, and physiological sensations (Chawla & Ostafin, 2007).
text.formatted: In contrast, psychological inflexibility and experiential avoidance involve rigid efforts to control, suppress, or escape unwanted thoughts, emotions, and physiological sensations <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Chawla & Ostafin, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Poor sleep may reduce individuals' capacity to flexibly respond to distress, while attempts to avoid or control uncomfortable internal experiences may further contribute to both sleep-related difficulties and internalizing symptoms (Dorrian et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Poor sleep may reduce individuals' capacity to flexibly respond to distress, while attempts to avoid or control uncomfortable internal experiences may further contribute to both sleep-related difficulties and internalizing symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Dorrian et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These processes are particularly relevant to depression and anxiety because avoidance can provide short-term relief while maintaining longer-term patterns of withdrawal, worry, and reduced engagement with reinforcing activities.
Sleep-specific cognitive and behavioral responses may also contribute to these relationships (Harvey, 2002).
text.formatted: Sleep-specific cognitive and behavioral responses may also contribute to these relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Harvey, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals experiencing sleep problems often develop maladaptive behaviors intended to compensate for or control poor sleep, such as altering activities based on anticipated fatigue, spending excessive time in bed, or rigidly attempting to manage sleep (Espie, 2002).

text.text: Similarly, dysfunctional beliefs and attitudes about sleep may amplify the perceived consequences of a poor night's sleep and increase cognitive and physiological arousal (Carney et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Similarly, dysfunctional beliefs and attitudes about sleep may amplify the perceived consequences of a poor night's sleep and increase cognitive and physiological arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Carney et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Although intended to manage sleep disturbance, such responses can perpetuate sleep difficulties and may contribute independently to psychological distress.

More broadly, dispositional characteristics associated with negative affectivity, internalizing tendencies, and social or emotional detachment may create shared vulnerability to both sleep disturbance and symptoms of depression or anxiety.
Despite a growing literature identifying potential explanatory processes, it has been difficult to determine which constructs are most relevant to the sleep-mental health relationship.
Candidate variables have often been examined individually, making it challenging to determine whether their associations persist when considered alongside competing constructs.
Moreover, statistical significance alone provides limited information about whether a candidate variable meaningfully contributes to an association between two constructs.

Variables may correlate significantly with insomnia and internalizing symptoms without substantially accounting for their shared variance, and constructs identified as explanatory variables may instead operate as moderators, consequences, or indicators of broader shared vulnerability.

These limitations are particularly important given substantial conceptual and empirical overlap among constructs such as emotion dysregulation, experiential avoidance, psychological inflexibility, and internalizing personality traits.

A recently proposed approach for evaluating associative variables provides a systematic method for identifying candidate processes when temporal or experimental data are not available to establish mediation (Weems, 2025).
text.formatted: A recently proposed approach for evaluating associative variables provides a systematic method for identifying candidate processes when temporal or experimental data are not available to establish mediation <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Weems, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Rather than relying on a single indirect-effect test, this approach evaluates candidate constructs across multiple criteria, including their zero-order relationships with predictor and outcome variables, unique associations when competing variables are considered simultaneously, incremental explanatory variance, attenuation of the original predictor-outcome association, bidirectional equivalence, and potential moderation.
Such an approach is particularly useful as an initial screening strategy for identifying constructs that warrant prioritization in subsequent longitudinal and experimental research.
Replication in an independent sample can further distinguish potentially robust associations from samplespecific findings.

The current study applied this framework to systematically evaluate psychological constructs that may help account for associations between insomnia symptoms and symptoms of depression and anxiety during emerging adulthood.
Using two independent samples, we first conducted exploratory analyses to identify candidate associative variables and then tested those variables in a larger independent confirmatory sample.

Candidate constructs included psychological flexibility, emotion regulation difficulties, experiential avoidance, maladaptive sleep-related behaviors and practices, and psychopathology dimensions (internalizing, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition, and anankastia) (Wright et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Candidate constructs included psychological flexibility, emotion regulation difficulties, experiential avoidance, maladaptive sleep-related behaviors and practices, and psychopathology dimensions (internalizing, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition, and anankastia) <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Wright et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Given the substantial overlap but also meaningful differences between depression and anxiety, associative variables were evaluated separately for each outcome.

We expected that more severe insomnia symptoms would be associated with greater symptoms of both depression and anxiety and that several transdiagnostic constructs (particularly emotion regulation difficulties, psychological inflexibility, and internalizing tendencies) would emerge as candidate associative variables.

By systematically comparing multiple candidate processes and evaluating their replication across independent samples, this study sought to identify the transdiagnostic psychological constructs most strongly associated with the sleep-depression/anxiety relationship and thereby prioritize targets for future longitudinal, experimental, and intervention research.
The overall study was in two parts.
In the first (Study 1), exploratory analyses were conducted to identify candidate constructs to be tested in the confirmatory study (Study 2).
Procedures Study 1 was conducted through recruitment of college students directly from two colleges or universities in the northeastern United States.
Students were eligible to participate if they were enrolled in the introduction to psychology research pools at the two schools.
Participants indicated interest in the project through Sona and completed the survey with Qualtrics.
They were compensated with course credit.
A total of N = 410 participants started the survey.
Of those, n = 44 did not complete key demographic questions (e.g., age, gender) and 60 failed at least two of the three attention check questions (e.g., "I sleep on a pillow made of spaghetti").
Given the overlap between those two categories, a total of n = 77 participants were excluded, leaving a sample of N = 333 who completed sufficient measures to be included in the analysis.

text.text: Depression and anxiety: Depression and anxiety were measured with the respective subscales from the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale (DASS-21).
The stress subscale was not used in this analysis, and was thus not presented to participants.

A total of 14 items were presented (seven each for depression and anxiety), and responses given on a four-point Likert-style scale ranging from zero ("Did not apply to me at all") to 3 ("Applied to me very much, or most of the time").
Depression items include statements like "I felt that I had nothing to look forward to", while anxiety items included statements like "I felt scared without any good reason."
In keeping with the original 42-item DASS, items within each subscale were summed and multiplied by two, with lower scores indicating lower levels of depression or anxiety.
Observed Cronbach alphas for Study 1 were acceptable, with .78 for anxiety and .90 for depression.
For Study 2, alphas were also acceptable, with .84 for anxiety and .92 for depression.
These values are about the same as in the original validating work (alpha = .88 for depression and .90 for anxiety) (Henry & Crawford, 2005).

text.text: Insomnia symptoms: Insomnia symptoms were measured by the Sleep Condition Indicator, a well-validated measure of insomnia.
The measure consists of eight Likert-style items such as "Thinking about a typical night in the past month, how long does it take you to fall asleep?", with five options.
The option reflecting the best sleep is scored a 4, while the option reflecting the worst sleep is scored a zero.
Higher scores reflect better sleep, unlike other commonly-used insomnia scales.
Observed Cronbach alpha for Study 1 was acceptable, alpha = .81, with a similar value for Study 2, alpha = .86.
These values are consistent with the alphas from the original validating work (alpha = .86) (Espie et al., 2014).

text.text: Acceptance of Sleep Difficulties: Acceptance of sleep difficulties was measured by the Sleep Problem Acceptance Questionnaire (SPAQ) (Bothelius et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Acceptance of Sleep Difficulties: Acceptance of sleep difficulties was measured by the Sleep Problem Acceptance Questionnaire (SPAQ) <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bothelius et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The measure consists of eight Likert-style items such as "I lead a full life even though I have sleeping problems," with responses scored from zero to six.
Note that several items are reverse scored, and the final scale is such that higher scores reflect more acceptance.
Although the scores can be summed to form a single acceptance score, both the original validating article and our analyses suggest a two-factor model.

One factor (AE) reflects active engagement (e.g., "Although things have changed, I am living a normal life despite my sleeping problems"), and the second reflects willingness to experience sleep problems (WILL; e.g., "It's important to keep on fighting these sleep problems", reversed).

Alphas in the original validating work were acceptable for the subscales (AE alpha = .89, with .73 for willingness), which were consistent with the results from our work (Study 1 AE alpha = .87, WILL alpha = .76; Study 2 AE alpha = .91, WILL alpha = .80).

text.text: Experiential Avoidance: Experiential avoidance is related to the psychological inflexibility measured by the AAQ2, but measures behaviors associated with avoiding distress or discomfort, as opposed to beliefs about the acceptability of distress and discomfort.
Experiential avoidance was measured with the Brief Experiential Avoidance Questionnaire (BEAQ), a 15-item, Likertstyle scale which includes items such as "I work hard to keep out upsetting feelings."
Each item is scored on a scale from one to six, and the total scale (after a single item reversal) is scored such that higher scores reflect greater behavioral avoidance.
Internal consistency from the original study was acceptable (alpha = .86), as was observed with our data (Study 1 alpha = .83; Study 2 alpha = .85).

text.text: To do this, we adopted the stepwise associational variable analysis approach described by Weems (Weems, 2025).
text.formatted: To do this, we adopted the stepwise associational variable analysis approach described by Weems <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Weems, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This approach screens candidate associative variables through a series of sequential steps.
In step one, we examined the zero-order correlations among sleep condition, each candidate associative variable, and the outcomes of depression and anxiety.
In step two, we conducted regression analyses to test three criteria.
First, including the associative variable had to explain a meaningful amount of additional variance in the outcome (ΔR² of .10 or greater).
Second, the association between sleep condition and the outcome (c) had to be meaningfully attenuated once the associative variable was included (c′).

Third, the association of the associative variable with the outcome (b) had to be comparable in strength to the association obtained when the model was reversed, with the associative variable regressed on the outcome (b′).
This last comparison shows that the results are not solely reliant on a directional interpretation.
In step three, we tested whether the associative variable instead moderated the relationship between sleep condition and the outcome.
Steps one and two are exclusionary: if a variable triplet did not meet the criteria at either step, it was not carried forward to Study 2.
Step three is expository and is meant to prompt consideration of moderation as an alternative explanation, rather than to exclude candidate variables.
Note that Weems (Weems, 2025) describes this as a four-step process; for simplicity and to reduce the number of tables, we report two of these steps together as step two.

text.text: We used a small exploratory study (N = 333) to identify candidate associative variables that may be a part, mechanistically or otherwise, of the relationship between sleep condition (SCI) and depression (DASS-depression) and/or anxiety (DASS-anxiety).
Because we had cross-sectional, non-experimental data, we used Weems' (Weems, 2025) approach, which is a step-wise screening to identify potential alternative explanations for the relationship.
After identifying candidate variable sets in the exploratory dataset, we replicated the analysis in a larger (N = 1,555) independent sample to confirm the exploratory findings.
The results were very similar.

These findings suggest that, for the relationship between sleep condition (SCI) and depression (DASS-depression), psychological flexibility (AAQ2) and emotion regulation (DERS) are the strongest candidates.

text.text: This study systematically screened a theoretically informed set of psychological constructs that might help account for associations between symptoms of insomnia and depression and between symptoms of insomnia and anxiety, using an exploratory sample followed by independent confirmation.
For depression, emotion regulation difficulties, psychological inflexibility, and behavioral avoidance emerged as robust candidate associative variables across the two samples.
For anxiety, emotion regulation difficulties and psychological inflexibility consistently met the path criteria across both samples.
Psychological inflexibility and emotion regulation difficulties may be particularly informative because they represent potentially modifiable processes.

Rather than suggesting different processes for depression and anxiety, the findings point to a combination of shared transdiagnostic processes and additional constructs that may be more specifically relevant to depression.
Psychological inflexibility may be an important transdiagnostic candidate linking sleep with internalizing symptoms.
Psychological inflexibility explained substantial incremental variance in both depression (ΔR² = .286) and anxiety (ΔR² = .182) in Study 2.

These findings are consistent with emerging literature linking greater psychological inflexibility with insomnia severity and poorer sleep quality across clinical and nonclinical samples (Ahn et al., 2024; El Rafihi-Ferreira et al., 2022; Zeng & Gan, 2026).
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with emerging literature linking greater psychological inflexibility with insomnia severity and poorer sleep quality across clinical and nonclinical samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ahn et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">El Rafihi-Ferreira et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Zeng & Gan, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Recent work examining specific dimensions of psychological inflexibility has similarly found associations between experiential avoidance, cognitive fusion, reduced present-moment awareness, and poorer sleep quality, in part through greater pre-sleep arousal (Mastin-Purcell et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Recent work examining specific dimensions of psychological inflexibility has similarly found associations between experiential avoidance, cognitive fusion, reduced present-moment awareness, and poorer sleep quality, in part through greater pre-sleep arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Mastin-Purcell et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Several processes could plausibly contribute to these associations.

Sleep difficulties may diminish individuals' capacity to respond flexibly to distressing internal experiences, while inflexible responses to fatigue, negative affect, or sleeprelated distress may contribute to rumination, withdrawal, and reduced engagement in valued activities.

Psychological inflexibility may therefore represent one candidate process relevant to the association of sleep difficulties with internalizing symptoms broadly, rather than with depression specifically.
However, given longstanding concerns regarding the construct and discriminant validity of the AAQ-II, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.

The AAQ-II has been criticized for substantial content and statistical overlap with negative affect and general psychological distress (Tyndall et al., 2019; Wolgast, 2014), raising the possibility that its comparatively strong associations with both depression and anxiety may partly reflect shared measurement content rather than a distinct transdiagnostic process.

text.text: Emotion regulation may represent a second potentially modifiable process relevant to associations between insomnia and internalizing symptoms.
Difficulties in emotion regulation demonstrated substantial incremental explanatory power for both depression (ΔR² = .277) and anxiety (ΔR² = .175) in Study 2.

Adequate sleep is thought to support adaptive emotion regulation, whereas sleep disruption and sleep loss have been associated with heightened emotional reactivity and diminished capacity to regulate negative affect (Gruber & Cassoff, 2014; Meneo et al., 2023; Palmer & Alfano, 2017).

text.text: A recent meta-analysis further demonstrated robust associations between insomnia symptoms and multiple dimensions of emotion dysregulation, including greater reliance on maladaptive regulatory strategies and dispositional difficulties in emotion regulation (Samea et al., 2025).

text.text: The current cross-sectional findings cannot establish the direction of these associations: sleep disturbance may compromise emotion regulation, emotion dysregulation may interfere with sleep, internalizing symptoms may contribute to both, or these processes may operate reciprocally over time.

The identification of emotion regulation as a candidate associative variable is nevertheless potentially important because emotion regulation is modifiable, providing a rationale for investigating these associations longitudinally and experimentally.
Some of the mental health benefits of successfully treating insomnia may occur in part because improvements in sleep restore greater capacity to regulate affect.

Consistent with this possibility, a recent randomized trial among adults with depressive symptoms found that digital cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) improved both emotion regulation difficulties and depressive symptoms relative to sleep hygiene education; moreover, early improvements in emotion regulation difficulties statistically mediated subsequent improvements in depression (Tamm et al., 2025).

text.text: Conversely, interventions that directly strengthen emotion regulation skills may have downstream benefits for both sleep and emotional symptoms.
Examining depression and anxiety separately revealed both shared and potentially symptomspecific patterns of association with insomnia.

Psychological inflexibility and emotion regulation difficulties survived the screening procedure for both outcomes, suggesting that these constructs may reflect processes relevant across internalizing symptoms.
In contrast, behavioral avoidance and detachment emerged as candidate associative variables for depression but not anxiety.

This pattern is conceptually consistent with models of depression emphasizing behavioral withdrawal and reductions in response-contingent positive reinforcement: avoidance can reduce engagement with rewarding or meaningful activities, while detachment similarly encompasses diminished social and emotional engagement, anhedonia, and reduced positive affect (Carvalho & Hopko, 2011; Dimidjian et al., 2011).

text.text: Together, these findings raise the possibility that insomnia intersects both with broad transdiagnostic processes and with constructs that may be more closely related to particular forms of internalizing psychopathology.

In particular, anxiety may involve additional sleep-relevant processes that were not well represented in the candidate set, including worry and repetitive negative thinking, intolerance of uncertainty, cognitive arousal, threat sensitivity, and anxiety sensitivity (Clancy et al., 2020; Harvey, 2002).

text.text: Several strengths of the present study increase confidence in the pattern of findings.

Rather than examining a single hypothesized explanatory variable in isolation, we systematically compared multiple theoretically plausible constructs using prespecified screening criteria that required more than statistical significance alone.
The use of an exploratory sample followed by an independent confirmatory sample provided an opportunity to determine which initial findings replicated in a separate and substantially larger sample.
Examining depression and anxiety separately further allowed us to distinguish constructs that emerged across both internalizing outcomes from those that appeared more specific to depression.

Finally, analyses considered competing explanations for observed associations, including moderation and reverse or bidirectional associations, providing a more comprehensive evaluation of the candidate variables than would a conventional cross-sectional mediation approach.
These strengths should be considered alongside several limitations.
Most importantly, both studies were cross-sectional and therefore cannot establish temporal ordering, mediation, or causality.
The prioritized constructs should consequently be understood as associative variables rather than demonstrated mechanisms.
All constructs were assessed using self-report measures, increasing the possibility that shared method variance contributed to observed associations.

Insomnia was assessed with the SCI, which captures insomnia symptoms but does not provide objective measures of sleep or represent the broader range of sleep disturbances that may relate to internalizing symptoms.
Similarly, the DASS assesses dimensional symptoms of depression and anxiety rather than clinical diagnoses; patterns of association may differ across specific depressive and anxiety disorders.
Interpretation is also complicated by potential conceptual and item-content overlap among several constructs.
This concern is particularly relevant to psychological inflexibility as measured by the AAQ-II, emotion dysregulation, internalizing, and the depression and anxiety outcomes.
Finally, although the candidate set was intentionally broad, it was not exhaustive.

Potentially important processes (including worry, repetitive negative thinking, and cognitive arousal) were not comprehensively represented, and the present results should not be interpreted as identifying all variables that may contribute to associations between insomnia and internalizing symptoms.
The number of candidate variables and analyses also raises the possibility of chance findings associated with multiple testing.

However, the structured screening procedure, requirement that candidates meet multiple criteria, and use of an independent exploratory-to-confirmatory design reduce concern that the principal findings reflect isolated statistically significant associations.

In conclusion, the present studies identified psychological inflexibility and emotion regulation difficulties as candidate associative variables relevant to both depression and anxiety in the context of insomnia symptoms, while behavioral avoidance emerged specifically for depression.

These findings illustrate the convergence of findings across an exploratory sample (N = 333) and a substantially larger independent confirmatory sample (overall N = 1,555, with analytic Ns varying by measure availability), strengthening confidence in the prioritized constructs and narrowing a broad theoretical space to a smaller set of candidates.

Longitudinal, experimental, and intervention studies are now needed to determine whether the identified candidates temporally or causally contribute to associations between sleep and emotional symptoms.

Clarifying these processes may ultimately help explain the broader mental health benefits of treating insomnia and identify additional targets for preventing the onset or recurrence of depression and anxiety among emerging adults.
